title: Is Complex Training Necessary for Long-Tailed OOD Detection? A Re-think from Feature Geometry
claim: Class-specific covariance and radial variation make distance scoring unreliable; projecting onto a sphere and pooling covariance gives stable, separable class clusters.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right; baseline panel, two parallel repair stages, merged result, legend strip
description: A wide figure with three columns, read left to right. The left panel, with a red-tinted border and titled 'Vanilla Mahalanobis', shows a 2-D scatter. Blue and green ID clusters sit inside elongated dashed ellipses, with orange OOD triangles scattered among and around them. Below the scatter are the distance formula d_M and red bullets saying the metric is unreliable. Arrows labelled 'Remove radial nuisance' and 'Pool cond-order evidence' fork to two stacked middle panels. The top panel, 'Hyperspherical Projection', shows clusters on a unit circle with the normalization formula. The bottom panel, 'Pooled Covariance Transform', shows a purple covariance heatmap and the Σ_pool formula. Both converge on the right panel, 'HPM: Projection + Pooled Metric', where compact circular clusters sit on concentric rings with OOD triangles near the centre. The d_HPM formula and bullets sit below. A legend strip along the bottom decodes the markers and ellipse styles. The caption below reads 'Mechanism of Hyperspherical Pooled Mahalanobis'.
caption: \HPM geometry repair. Class-conditional Mahalanobis is unstable when tail classes lack residual support (top path). \HPM first projects features to the hypersphere to remove radial bias correlated with imbalance, then uses pooled residual covariance to replace tail-specific spectra with shared, ridge-regularized geometry while preserving class mean anchors.
abstract: Long-tailed out-of-distribution (LT-OOD) detection is often addressed with specialized training, including auxiliary out-of-distribution (OOD) data, abstention heads, contrastive objectives, energy losses, or gradient-conflict control. We show that these training mechanisms can obscure a simpler issue: frozen long-tailed representations may already contain useful OOD evidence, but raw Mahalanobis distance is distorted by frequency-coupled feature radius and poorly supported tail covariance. We propose Hyperspherical Pooled Mahalanobis (HPM), a post-hoc detector that normalizes features onto the unit sphere and replaces class-specific covariance with a pooled, ridge-regularized metric while keeping class means as semantic anchors. In CIFAR-LT experiments and an ImageNet-100-LT near-OOD boundary analysis, HPM improves raw Mahalanobis scoring; for Prior-Calibrated ERM (PC-ERM), it raises AUROC from 46.49 to 85.67 on CIFAR-10-LT and from 50.40 to 78.35 on CIFAR-100-LT. This simple PC-ERM+HPM pipeline also achieves the best Log Efficiency Score (LES; 3.08) on CIFAR-100-LT, retaining roughly 95% of the best CIFAR-100-LT AUROC observed among the compared post-hoc scores at substantially lower training-time cost. These results argue for evaluating representation quality, detector geometry, and training complexity as separate factors in LT-OOD detection.
